item.title: What Happens If Your Passport Expires While You're Abroad?
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler
Most countries don't allow international travelers to enter their territory unless they have at least six months left before their passport expires. That might sound like an unnecessary ask for a week-long vacation, but the rule is in place for good reason. That's because if you do find yourself in a scenario when your passport expires while you're abroad—say due to an unexpected medical issue or trip delay, for example—you could be facing a major bureaucratic headache. However, although it might feel like a crisis, having your passport lapse while traveling is not the end of the world. There are procedures that travelers can follow to obtain a renewed document and get their trip back on track. Here’s a look at what happens if your passport expires while you’re abroad. How far in advance should I renew my passport? Many countries do not allow international tourists to visit unless they have a certain amount of validity left on their passport. A common rule of thumb that many nations observe is the six month rule: there must be at least six months before your passport expires in order to enter the country. In some countries, including many popular destinations in the EU, your passport is required to be valid for an additional three months after your intended departure date. Before you board an international flight, airlines will verify your passport expiration and usually will not let you board the plane if your passport doesn’t meet the validity requirements. It's important to note that some airlines and cruise lines might have their own passport validity policies that differ from the country's official requirements, so be sure to check both. What to do if your passport expires while you’re abroad Sometimes, it’s possible to enter a different country and stay past your passport’s expiration date. If that's the case, the protocol you’ll need to follow is similar to when a passport is lost or stolen abroad. First, you’ll need to contact the nearest US embassy or consulate for assistance. If you’re not sure where the nearest embassy or consulate might be, you can use the search tool on the State Department’s website. You’ll need to then visit the embassy or consulate location in person in order to have them issue you a new passport. Keep in mind this could mean you need to travel to a different city within the country you’re visiting. When you arrive, you’ll essentially need to apply for a new passport. That means you’ll need to bring: - Identification such as a driver's license or expired passport - Proof of U.S. citizenship (like an expired passport) - Travel itinerary from your airline or train tickets - Completed DS-11 Application for Passport document “Even if you cannot present all these documents, consular staff will do their best to help you get a new passport quickly,” the State Department’s site says. US citizens abroad who have urgent travel plans are usually issued an emergency passport, which is valid for up to one year. However, it’s also possible to get a full-validity passport that doesn’t expire for 10 years. It will depend on the specifics of your situation. Replacement passports are usually issued by the next business day, according to the State Department. If you’re a US citizen living overseas for an extended period of time, you might qualify for routine passport renewal by mail through the nearest US embassy or consulate. Processing times for renewal by mail are usually about four to six weeks, not including shipping time. Visit the website of the local embassy or consulate in your area and follow their instructions for passport renewal. Here are a few helpful protocols to help avoid passport issues when traveling abroad: - Before departure, always check your passport expiration date and the passport validity rules for tourist visas for each country you’re visiting. - Familiarize yourself with the locations of US embassies and consulates in the countries where you’ll be traveling. - Travel with a photo or photocopy of your passport’s bio page in case it is lost or stolen. - Plan to renew your passport at least six to nine months before it expires. Many travelers can now do this online in the US, which makes the process easier than ever.

item.title: Copenhagen is Opening a Stunning New Bathhouse Along Its Harbor This December—And It's Shockingly Affordable
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler
Copenhagen is a swimmer’s city. "The cure for anything is salt water: sweat, tears, or the sea," Danish author Karen Blixen, who lived up the coast from Copenhagen, famously wrote in 1934. Locals and visitors alike have taken her words to heart ever since. In the early 2000s, floating swimming pools were introduced to the Danish capital's harbor after the city's shipbuilding industry collapsed. These pools turned an unused space into a playground for swimmers, divers, water polo enthusiasts, and boaters, especially on hot summer days. In recent years, cold plunging has also risen in popularity as a way to help with mental and physical health—nowadays, you can expect winter swimming clubs with sauna access along the harbor to have lengthy waiting lists. The next time you visit Copenhagen, there's even more reason to pack a swimsuit. The city’s historic waterfront welcomes a long-awaited new addition on Saturday, December 5: a public swimming pool set to become a new landmark along the city's harbor. Designed by the Japanese architectural firm Kengo Kuma Associates, Kai is the new 62,500 square-foot bathing house that has been eight years in the making. It promises ten pools in total, including an open-air rooftop pool and a heated onsen overlooking Copenhagen Harbor. Delayed due to the pandemic and its knock-on effects, the pool was originally slated to open in 2021 and now joins the list of architecturally distinct buildings lining Copenhagen Harbor, including the modern Opera House and the Royal Danish Playhouse. Pools will be spread across the several levels of the minimalist interior, with a 82-foot pool on the ground floor. The building also offers year-round access to the harbor with designated swimming and dipping zones in and around a timber boardwalk. While the harbor itself can get pretty chilly in winter, the outdoor first-floor pools benefit from a sustainable vertical ground-source heat pump system providing year-round heating. This designer swimming experience comes with a surprisingly affordable price tag for visitors. Tickets are expected to be in line with other local city-run swimming pools—known as "water culture houses"—where entry is typically under 100kr (about $10). Capacity overall is capped at 380 swimmers. The 989 million DKK ($150 million) project was funded by the City of Copenhagen and Nordea Fonden. Swimmers all over the city are delighted with the news, including Copenhagen’s Lord Mayor Sisse Marie Welling. “I’m really excited about the opening of the Water Culture House,” she said. “Copenhagen needs more swimming facilities, so it’s incredibly important that we are now getting new pools for adults, as well as paddling pools for children. I hope it will become the city’s new gathering point for water-loving Copenhageners and visitors alike.” The original idea for a new pool in the heart of the city came directly from Copenhageners. Surveys had pinpointed a desire for a new, central public swimming pool and the location on Paper Island could not be better. Once the site of a beloved food market, the area had stood empty for years, before being redeveloped to play home to restaurants, cafes and hospitality businesses. Directly across the harbor from the central tourist hub of Nyhavn and accessed by pedestrian and cycle bridge, the new pool brings renewed focus to the area, that links the old town with the rapidly gentrifying former military area of Holmen and the former shipbuilding area of Refshaleøen. More of the best bathhouses in Copenhagen If you are keen to explore Copenhagen’s swimming cultures, the harbor is the place to start—but brace yourself for chilly waters. At Sandkaj in Nordhavn in the north of the city, a demarcated swim zone invites bathers directly into the deep harbor for lane swimming. It’s a great place for a chat with a fellow winter swimmer; changing room access is members-only, but there is space to change on the quay. Warm up with a sauna at Saunanor, where you can also try the distinctive Danish saunagus tradition. Those seeking a more spa-like experience should head up the coast to Skodsborg Spa Hotel. The former sanatorium offers a superlative spa experience with 16 different bathing experiences, including saunas, steam rooms and access to a private swimming jetty on the beach. Alternative public swimming spots include Valby’s Water Culture House, a chic grey building a world away from typical leisure centre design with a slide, lane swimming and a hot pool area. This article was originally published on Condé Nast Traveller UK.

item.title: Where was War filmed? Inside the glamorous London locations of the new HBO series
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler UK
On Location peels back the curtain on some of your favourite films, television shows, and more. This time, we ask: where was War filmed? London very rarely gets the glossy treatment on the small screen, but this autumn’s hottest new drama, War, has put an end to that. That’s because the eight-part series is set within the glamorous world of high-stakes celebrity divorce, with Sienna Miller and Dominic West playing the uber-rich couple at the heart of the case. Not only do Miller and West’s characters inhabit luxurious spaces (often barely lived in), but so too do their respective law firms. Indeed, the offices of Cathcarts (representing West’s Morgan Henderson) and Taylor & Bryne (representing Miller’s Carla Duval) are the epitome of Old Money vs New Money, with the architecture and decor to match. Production designer Debbie Burton was keen to ensure that this was London as we’d never seen it before. “I didn’t want the Shard in the background of every shot, for example,” she explains. “London is much more interesting than that. It’s a city where historic architecture – whether Georgian, Victorian or neoclassical – exists alongside glass and steel, and finding locations where those worlds could exist together became a really useful visual reference.” When it came to finding the perfect locations for the law firms, she thought about what each represented, and how that would translate to where they worked. “Initially, what was on the page – and what became clearer through research and preparing the pitch – was that there were two very different law firms and two very different worlds,” she says. “Cathcarts represented old-established heritage: a firm that had existed for hundreds of years and had been passed down through generations. It felt cloistered and secretive. Taylor & Byrne, on the other hand, was much more about openness, transparency and light. It was an obvious visual contrast between the two worlds.” For Cathcarts, she settled on a Victorian exterior, with a more Art Deco interior. “It wasn’t necessarily claustrophobic, but there was a sense of being enclosed,” she explains. “The idea was that the footprint of the building remained consistent across several floors, so we could create the impression that we were moving through this one large world.” The opposite was true of Taylor & Bryne, which is more modern and open-plan. “The exterior was essentially one big glass-and-steel box, so I wanted to bring some structural elements into the set design,” she says. “We spent a lot of time looking at office lobbies around London and rejecting them because they felt too generic or over-designed. A lot of modern spaces have elements that immediately date them, things like grass walls, and we wanted something cleaner. Eventually we found somewhere in Canary Wharf that worked because it had scale and impact, but it was also clean and understated.” When it came to the homes of Carla and Morgan, she wanted them to feel authentic to their characters. For Carla, this meant a space that was chic and spoke to her glamorousness, while for Morgan, it was more impersonal – he’s someone who frequently stays in hotel penthouses around the world and so nowhere really feels that lived in. “He’s someone who can pick up a bag and go wherever he needs to go. His spaces needed to reflect that transient, international lifestyle,” she says. And while the crew have been tight-lipped on the exact filming locations, here are some that have been confirmed. Where was War filmed? One of the most memorable scenes of the series takes place at the end of the first episode, and sees Carla served with divorce papers while attending the premiere of her latest film in London. The dramatic moment was shot on the South Bank, outside the British Film Institute, which can be seen in the background. We are introduced to one of the show’s most important characters, aspiring lawyer Johnny (Archie Renaux) when he is working as a waiter at an upmarket restaurant, the fictional Zinzolin. It is here that he is antagonised by his girlfriend Bella’s obnoxious friend, Angus, with the resulting fight leading to Johnny losing his job. These scenes were shot at Brasserie Zedel, the sprawling subterranean French restaurant underneath Piccadilly Circus, which is a favourite among media types who work nearby. Before they go down the messy court case route, Carla and Morgan must first undergo arbitration, in an attempt to settle their divorce amicably. The rather grand setting for this is called Marlborough House in the show, whereas in real life, the scenes were filmed at Skinners’ Hall on Dowgate Hill off Cannon Street. The Grade I-listed building is home to the Skinners Association, a philanthropic membership organisation with hundreds of years of history. Throughout the series, Carla strategises with Serena, her lawyer, et al from her rather chic living room. These scenes were actually filmed at an event space at the three-star Columbia Hotel in Lancaster Gate, which comprises five Victorian townhouses joined together. “It was that architecture that was really important to get a sense of history so that we feel like it isn’t just a transient space,” Burton told Galerie Magazine. “I wanted it to feel very much designed by Carla, because she’s the style icon of the show. She’s knowledgeable about design, and she’s well-travelled. She has influences from all over.” Many of the pieces seen in Carla’s home were sourced at nearby Sunbury Antiques Market in Kempton, including chinoiserie and sideboards. The husband and wife founders of Taylor & Bryne, Nick and Serena (played by James McArdle and Phoebe Fox) live in the kind of gentrified Victorian townhouse associated with higher-income earners in the capital. The scenes filmed in their home were reportedly shot in a house in Maida Vale, which is known for being particularly affluent and leafy. In episode five, we find ourselves in Morgan Henderson’s place of work, as we see inside the offices of his social media company, Zephyr HQ. The Grade II-listed modernist building is affectionately known as “the Hanging Gardens of Basingstoke,” thanks in large part to its combination of 1970s brutalist architecture and unique roof gardens.

item.title: Exclusive: American Express adds high-yield savings account deposits as new Reward Dollars redemption method
item.description:
Source: The Points Guy
If you hold either the Blue Cash Everyday® Card from American Express or the Blue Cash Preferred® Card from American Express, you now have a new way to redeem your Reward Dollars: as a deposit into an American Express high-yield savings account (HYSA). American Express is also extending a similar redemption option to business cardmembers. Starting Oct. 29, Graphite™ Business Cash Unlimited Card cardholders can redeem Reward Dollars into an Amex Business Checking account. Both redemption options are available at a 1:1 rate, meaning $100 in Reward Dollars can become a $100 deposit into an eligible Amex bank account. Whether you're saving for an emergency, a dream trip or your kid's college fund, this is a great new way to make your cash back work for you. Here's what you need to know. Redeem your Amex Reward Dollars for a high-yield savings account deposit You can easily redeem your Reward Dollars for a deposit into your Amex high-yield savings account online or by calling Amex. Of course, you must have an open HYSA with Amex to use this redemption method. If you don't already have an Amex HYSA, you can apply for one during the redemption process. You must have either the Blue Cash Everyday or the Blue Cash Preferred to use your rewards this way. Cash back on these cards is earned as Reward Dollars that can be redeemed as a statement credit, for a deposit into an FDIC-Insured American Express High Yield Savings Account or at Amazon.com checkout. Meanwhile, Graphite Business Cash Unlimited cardmembers can redeem their Reward Dollars for deposits into an Amex Business Checking account. I view this as a worthwhile redemption, since it's a great way to boost any savings fund you already have or kickstart a new one. Since Reward Dollars can't be converted into Amex Membership Rewards points, you don't need to worry about transfer partners to maximize the value you receive with each redemption. And, there's no minimum redemption option. Starting in 2027, Amex also plans to introduce automatic Reward Dollars deposits into eligible consumer cardmembers' HYSAs. The issuer hasn't yet shared whether cardmembers will be able to choose the amount or frequency of those deposits. Why Amex is expanding its banking redemption options The new redemption options are part of American Express's broader efforts to connect its credit cards, rewards and banking products. In responses provided to TPG via email, Corey Timlin, Amex's head of consumer banking, said the company is seeing growing engagement with its banking products, particularly among younger customers. According to Timlin, U.S. consumer and small-business banking deposit balances grew 9% year over year in the second quarter of 2026, with the majority of deposits coming from cardmembers. Millennials and Gen Z also represent more than half of Amex's HYSA accounts and approximately one-third of balances. Timlin said these trends helped inform the new redemption option, which makes it easier for eligible cardmembers to turn their rewards into savings. While Amex hasn't announced plans to allow cash-back cardmembers to convert Reward Dollars into Membership Rewards points, Timlin said the company sees opportunities to continue connecting its cards, rewards and banking products. Is it worth opening an American Express high-yield savings account? It's good financial practice to have a high-yield savings account, even if you aren't able to save a substantial amount each month. While some checking accounts offer interest, you'll generally receive a better return with a HYSA. There are no opening or monthly fees associated with Amex's HYSA. Your interest compounds daily and is paid out monthly. As of Oct. 28, Amex's HYSA offers a 3.20% annual percentage yield (APY), although the rate is variable and subject to change. This is fairly standard for HYSAs, making it a great spot to park your savings. If you already have a competitive HYSA elsewhere, you may prefer to redeem your Reward Dollars as a statement credit and put the equivalent savings into your existing account. How much cash back can I earn with an eligible Amex card? The no-annual-fee Blue Cash Everyday (see rates and fees) earns 3% cash back on the following categories: - U.S. supermarkets (on the first $6,000 in spending each calendar year, then 1% back) - U.S. online retail purchases (on the first $6,000 in spending each calendar year, then 1% back) - U.S. gas stations (on the first $6,000 in spending per calendar year, then 1% back) Meanwhile, the $95-per-year ($0 introductory annual fee for the first cardmember year) Blue Cash Preferred (see rates and fees) offers more robust earning rates: - 6% cash back at U.S. supermarkets (on the first $6,000 in spending each calendar year, then 1% back) - 6% cash back on select U.S. streaming subscriptions Both cards earn 1% cash back on purchases made outside their bonus categories. The Blue Cash Everyday will likely be sufficient for many, but if you spend a substantial amount each year on groceries and transit, you'll appreciate the Blue Cash Preferred's earning rates more. If you maximize either card's U.S. groceries category, as an example, you'd earn $180 in cash back with the Blue Cash Everyday and $360 back with the Blue Cash Preferred. For business owners, the Graphite Business Cash earns unlimited 2% cash back on eligible purchases, with no cap. All three cards earn cash back as Reward Dollars, but the new bank deposit options differ. Eligible consumer cash-back cardmembers can redeem into an Amex HYSA, while Graphite Business Cash Unlimited cardmembers can redeem into an Amex Business Checking account. If you're a current or prospective Blue Cash Everyday or Blue Cash Preferred cardholder, you now have the option to redeem your Reward Dollars for a deposit into your Amex high-yield savings account. If you're team cash-back, this is a great opportunity to bolster your savings account for whatever goal you have in mind. And business owners who carry the Graphite Business Cash Unlimited can also redeem their rewards into an Amex Business Checking account. The new options won't necessarily make your Reward Dollars worth more, since they redeem at a 1:1 rate. However, they provide a convenient way to put cash back toward savings or everyday banking needs. Of course, you can still redeem your Reward Dollars for a statement credit or at Amazon checkout, if those are the redemption methods you prefer. Either way, having a cash-back card can help your dollars stretch a lot further. To learn more, check out our full reviews of the Blue Cash Everyday and Blue Cash Preferred.

item.title: Survive Unexpected Winter Storms on the Trail With These 5 Expert Tips
item.description:
Source: Backpacker Magazine
The best way to survive a winter storm is to not get caught in one. True as that may be, however, it’s not a very useful tip when the snow has already started falling. As weather grows more unpredictable, getting stuck on the trail, even when you’ve dutifully checked the forecasts, could happen to any of us. The key to surviving is always being prepared for the worst by packing the 10 essentials and reading articles like this, even if you’re just planning to go on a day hike. “If you ask me what’s the highest risk, it’s those short hikes because they’re the ones most people aren’t prepared for the longer term,” says Dan Wowak of Coalcracker Bushcraft, a wilderness school and YouTube channel based in Pennsylvania. “A two-mile hike can turn into a devastating emergency situation. You roll an ankle, a storm comes in, it gets dark, you have no equipment, and you don’t know what to do.” We talked to Wowak and two other experienced hikers about what to do when bad weather rolls in with no warning. The first step: They all suggest packing the right things for winter, including an emergency shelter, communication device, extra layers, navigation, and a fire starter. You might think that if you’re only a mile from the trailhead, you’re home free. But as snow starts to cover the trail and any tracks you may have left, you might as well be days away. “When you’re out and the weather is turning, you might be inclined to go faster,” says Danny Giovale, the founder of Kahtoola. “I would strongly suggest stopping for a sec.” Knowing when to stop and wait out the storm will save you from precarious situations. Giovale and Wowak suggest considering how far you have left to go and the time of day. If the storm is moving in quickly and it’s getting dark, it’s best to stop and prioritize survival. Nighttime, Wowak says, is one of the worst times to travel because both visibility and temperatures are at their lowest. So if dusk approaches and you’re not prepared with the equipment and knowledge to travel in the dark, settle in to spend the night out there. If you packed an emergency bivy or a tent, it’s crucial to set that up immediately to protect yourself from the elements, like snow, rain, and wind. Blocking the weather is going to prolong your survival timeline. “If you’re not dry, you’re in trouble really fast,” says Jon King, who hikes daily and sends the trail report for 10,000-footer San Jacinto Peak in California. If you don’t have shelter, Giovale suggests looking for a cave or building your own in the snow. This, of course, requires prior knowledge, but the idea is to create a big pile of snow. Let it set up into a dome and then dig out a space for your body. Don’t forget to poke an air vent. Then there are trails with man-made shelters, like on San Jacinto Peak, says King. Part of your preparation is knowing where these huts and structures are located in case you ever need them. As your hands grow cold, they become less functional. As your body loses heat, you become at risk for developing hypothermia and making rash decisions. In addition to a shelter, Giovale always brings a lightweight shell jacket with a hood. It’s “one of the ounce-per-ounce most impactful pieces of gear,” he says. Staying as dry as possible with extra layers will keep you warm. Keep exercising and moving to stimulate blood flow to your fingers and toes. Wowak also recommends building a fire. “Getting a campfire started is a very relaxing and primal thing that makes people feel safe in just about any situation,” he says. Some caveats apply. It’s harder to do in a torrential downpour than in a snowstorm. It’s also not always advised in fire-prone areas or during a fire ban unless it’s a life-or-death situation. Should you spend the night outside, make sure to insulate your body from the ground so you don’t lose body heat, he adds. A foam mat will work, but in lieu of that, so will pine boughs. In a pinch, you can sit on your backpack. Ration your water reserves to stay hydrated, or use the campfire to melt snow and warm up a drink. Drinking cold water can drain your energy, Wowak says, so warm water is better. Unless you brought snacks, you might start to feel hunger pangs. Hydration can help there, too. “,Even if we don’t have a lot of food, if we were only planning on a day hike and a storm comes in, and we’re stuck there, being hydrated will trick your body and you won’t feel as hungry because you’re full of fluid,” Wowak says. The worst thing you can do in any kind of survival scenario is dwell on the situation, Wowak says. Keep your mind engaged with survival tasks like making your camp bed, boiling water, organizing your gear, moving your toes and fingers, etcetera. Giovale says to trust your prior training to get you through the storm. “My experience with being in serious situations outside is that whatever you have learned or been exposed to, you’ll probably remember,” he says.

item.title: A hotel with a thrill ride? Hyatt is taking Times Square to new heights
item.description:
Source: The Points Guy
Hyatt is aiming for the sky in New York City. The company announced a flagship property for the StandardX brand set to occupy a supertall skyscraper currently under construction in Midtown Manhattan. Dubbed The StandardX Times Square, the hotel will feature 1,800 rooms, making it the largest Hyatt property in NYC and one of the largest hotels in the city. What's most interesting about The StandardX Times Square, however, is actually what's outside of the rooms. The property will feature a rooftop pool (a rarity in NYC), an observation deck over 1,000 feet in the air and, most exciting, "an enclosed free-fall thrill ride," according to a statement from Hyatt. The StandardX, the "rebellious younger sibling" brand of The Standard, was launched in 2023 with its first location opening later in Melbourne, Australia. Hyatt describes the brand as a toned-down version of The Standard with all of the heart: "Great beds, good design, interesting people and a connection to the city outside. The rooms are simpler, the service more casual and the experience more streamlined," Hyatt said in the statement. Considering its location right off Times Square and in the Theater District, the hotel will be inspired by "New York's theatrical character," with straightforward but expressive rooms and public spaces designed to "bring together the design, music and social energy associated with The Standard." Besides the attractions sure to draw in thrillseekers and tourists alike, the hotel will also feature a "substantial" series of restaurants, bars and nightlife venues in the Extell Development Company-backed building dubbed "The Torch." "The Standard brand has always been about being part of the city," Amar Lalvani, chief creative officer at Hyatt and president and director of Hyatt Lifestyle Group, said in the statement. "With StandardX hotels, we’ve taken that same idea and made it simpler and more accessible. Usually, that means putting people in the middle of an interesting neighborhood, with everything happening right outside the door. In Times Square, a lot of it will be happening right inside the building." Hyatt was quick to point out that The StandardX Times Square will be a one-off flagship location rather than a model for other StandardX properties. Or, as Lalvani put it, they wanted to "create something that could only happen in New York." The StandardX Times Square is scheduled to open in the second half of 2028. Related reading:

item.title: Why are Thai restaurants hidden in London pubs?
item.description:
Source: BBC Travel
Why are so many Thai restaurants hidden inside London pubs? Three pints into a crisp evening in west London, I'm standing outside The Churchill Arms pub with some British friends, and I'm getting hungry. "We can just eat here. I've booked us a table at the Thai restaurant in the back," a friend says. Maybe it's the ale talking, or the jet lag from my New York flight, but I'm confused. "There's a Thai restaurant here?" I ask. "In the back of the pub?" My friends whisk me past the bar, where model British war planes, flags and World War Two-era military photographs fill the walls. But as we approach the backroom, Union Jacks turn into Trairong – the tricolour Thai flag – and woven rattan baskets, small boat oars and old kanok metal lanterns dangle from the ceiling. We pass a busy kitchen filled with the clang of pots and woks, and a Thai waiter leads us to a table in what feels like a tropical greenhouse. Lush ferns dangle from the ceiling, while bright red and yellow flowers sprout from planters and pictures of exotic butterflies cover the walls. Looking back towards the dark, wood-panelled British pub in the next room, I feel as though I've been transported somewhere else. In reality, I've just stepped into one of London's most unique dining experiences: a Thai restaurant tucked into a traditional British or Irish bar, cheekily known as a "Thai-rish" pub. Though well-known among London barflies, many visitors may be surprised to learn that roughly 30 Thai restaurants operate out of the hidden backrooms and upstairs lofts of traditional English or Irish-run pubs. At first glance, these portmanteau pubs may seem like a rather unlikely pairing, but over the decades, these fusion businesses have become a distinctive feature of the city's pub culture – and as I'd soon learn, the idea was born right here at The Churchill Arms. According to BBC Radio London's restaurant contributor, Stephanie Brookes, Thai cuisine wasn't on most Londoners' radars back in the 1980s, but the city's tastes were changing. At most pubs, "food was once an afterthought", Brookes says, remembering the ham-and-cheese toasties and packets of crisps served in her youth. At the time, there weren't many Thai restaurants in London, but as Thailand became a popular backpacking destination for young Brits in the late 1980s and '90s, more travellers returned with a taste for Thai food. "[People who wanted to] try new cuisines and experience different flavours had that opportunity – it's inevitable that tastes [back home in Britain] would start to change as a result," Brookes says. "This was partly a backlash against the bland food and austerity that came before." The Churchill Arms' current manager James Keogh, remembers how the unlikely idea of serving pints alongside pad Thai was born. As he recalls, an Irishman named Gerry O'Brien moved to London in 1985, taking up ownership of the Kensington establishment. At the time, the bar just served fish and chips, jacket potatoes and other classic British pub grub. O'Brien was searching for a way to liven up the menu when Thai chef Songkot Boonyasarayon asked him if he could cook in the pub's kitchen. O'Brien was initially hesitant, but once he tried Boonyasarayon's cooking, he agreed to a month-long trial in the summer of 1988. Within a few weeks, London food and restaurant writer Nick Lander recalls that there were lines around the block. "[O'Brien] just thought it would be something that would work for a few months and that would be it," says Lander, who met O'Brien in 2009. "I don't think he had any idea of it being so popular." By the early 2000s, the Thai government had launched the Global Thai Campaign, an early example of "gastrodiplomacy" aimed at promoting Thai cuisine around the world. As part of it, the government provided loans to Thai citizens to relocate and share their culture abroad, and within the next decade, the number of Thai restaurants around the world nearly doubled. In the UK, many Thai chefs were hired in bar kitchens, with some chefs fully taking over day-to-day culinary operations or converting backrooms into a restaurant inside the pubs. Soon, Thai-rish pubs began to take off elsewhere in London. "Many [Thai-rish] pubs rival top restaurants in terms of quality and provenance of ingredients," says Brookes. As I scan the menu at The Churchill Arms, I spot dishes like (stir-fried "drunken noodles") and a special duck curry made with red chilli and coconut milk. I opt for the (red curry stir-fry), whose rich braise, bold spices and sharp acidity balance well with the malty sweetness of traditional English and Irish beers. "Its model is perfect, if you think about it," Brookes says. "Delicious ingredients that are easy to prepare in a relatively small kitchen space, and the aromatic flavours work incredibly well with a crisp, light beer." Kate, a London foodie who posts about Thai food in pubs on TikTok, agrees: "Thai food and pubs are two of the world's greatest things that only become stronger when in tandem with each other," she tells me. "Thai food mixes the sweet, spicy, sour and salty, and pubs mix drinking, danger and questionable decisions. What more of a powerful combination could you ask for?" Ryan McElhinney, owner of The King's Arms near London Bridge, moved from Ireland in 2001 to help his father run the pub and remembers how they started serving Thai food. "[At the time] if my friends ever came to visit, I wouldn't recommend them to have food at our pub, because I knew it was just average… [things like] sausage and mash," he says. Shortly after, McElhinney's brother met and married a Thai woman. She soon took over the kitchen, and by 2002, the pub was serving Thai food. "Our Thai food got better and better. We had Thai chefs making the food, and the food they have is amazing," says McElhinney, comparing the daily stream of curries such massaman and panang to the anticipation of "Christmas morning". Today, McElhinney co-owns multiple pubs across London, and they all serve Thai food. He maintains that pad Thai and spice bags (its chips tossed with spices, stir-fried vegetables and chicken) remain their most popular dishes: "You gotta give the customers what they want… but alcohol and spicy food and a bit of salt, it lends itself." In Nunhead, south-east London, Irish pub Skehans serves Thai food from a kitchen managed by Thai chef Charlene "Chai" Skehan. She moved to London from Thailand age 13, learning English and training in various pub kitchens. Twenty-five years ago, she and her husband Bill took over the pub and opened Chai's Garden Restaurant at the back. "Thai food paired naturally with beer, particularly Singha and Tiger, although I'm surprised by how well the beef dishes went with Guinness," she says. Chai's kitchen has provided a pathway for numerous Thai chefs in London. All her chefs come from Thailand, recruited through connections she has built throughout her time in London. Two of them have worked alongside her for more than 20 years and can still be found cooking at Skehans. Others have been trained up in her kitchen and gone on to work in nearby pubs, contributing to the presence of Thai kitchens across London. As we finish our fragrant curries, stir fries and ales in the backroom of The Churchill Arms, I think about something Chai said. "Thai food belongs in the pub." – a handpicked selection of features, videos and can't-miss news, delivered to your inbox twice a week.

item.title: IDEA: Hubbard Glacier vs. Glacier Bay: Which is the better scenic cruising spot in Alaska?
item.description:
Source: The Points Guy
Cruising in Alaska means you want to see all the things. The list includes whales, sled dogs and bald eagles. You want stunning scenery and informative tours. Topping most people’s list is glacier viewing. It’s an intrinsic part of what we hope to see on a cruise in Alaska waters — perhaps even the main reason to choose a cruise or cruisetour rather than an exclusively land-based Alaska vacation. Cruise lines get that and dedicate time to cruising near the region’s most famous rivers of ice in an effort to make everyone’s dreams of glacial awe come true. But how do you know which Alaska cruise itinerary will get you the most close-up time with the best glaciers? Let’s start with the top two choices for most Alaska cruisers: Hubbard Glacier and Glacier Bay National Park and Preserve. There are cruises that visit both, but often, you must choose between them when booking your cruise. My vote goes to Glacier Bay, but before we dive into the details to back up my choice, let’s go over the basics of choosing an Alaska glacier cruise. Tips to ensure you see a glacier on your cruise You need to know that it is entirely possible to book a cruise in Alaska that does not take you to any glacier. I’ve done that and had a wonderful time. It’s important to remember, though, that even routes that plan for glacier time can come up short. Weather, ice in the water and onboard emergencies are the usual reasons ships must skip scheduled glacier visits. My glacierless cruise was not an accident or a surprise. It was an early season, short cruise that only visited Ketchikan, Alaska, and Victoria, British Columbia. If it’s glaciers you seek, plan accordingly with these three tips to improve your chances. - Book a midseason cruise; early and late-season cruises face more ice in the water and more challenging weather conditions. - Choose a cruise with more than one glacier cruising day to double your odds. - Add a glacier cruising excursion; these are often possible from the ports before or after the day your ship plans to do its scenic cruising near a glacier. Tip: If your cruise offers a glacier-viewing excursion on the day the ship is scheduled for scenic cruising near a glacier, take it. It indicates that the ship won't get as close as you might want. Here’s what to expect from the two most popular glacier destinations. It's the longest tidewater glacier in North America, with a face more than 400 feet high and almost 7 miles wide. The majority of cruise lines that visit Alaska include Hubbard Glacier on at least one itinerary — most often on one-way sailings or 10- to 14-night cruises. Remember that only a handful of 7-night, round-trip cruises include Hubbard Glacier. The list includes Alaska newcomer Virgin Voyages, as well as small- and medium-ship cruise lines like Crystal, Silversea and The Ritz-Carlton Yacht Collection. Hubbard Glacier's enormous face is its biggest draw. Its massive size means you can see it even on visits when the ship cannot get as close as you'd like. Ships typically get within a quarter- to a half-mile of the face of the glacier, but the amount of ice in the water can sometimes force ships to halt farther out in the fjord. Hubbard is sometimes called "The Galloping Glacier" because it has been advancing into Disenchantment Bay for more than 100 years — sometimes in surges that cut off nearby Russell Fjord. It is currently considered stable in terms of overall size, but it's steadily moving forward into the bay. That movement causes ice to break off and fall into the sea in a process known as calving, which is not related as much to temperature as it is to the physics of the glacier's thickness and the steepness of the land mass it crosses. Ice chunks the size of three-story buildings often fall into the water, creating a thunderous roar and waves that pound nearby shorelines. The glacier is part of 13.2 million-acre Wrangell-St. Elias National Park and Preserve, a UNESCO World Heritage Site. The park encompasses the largest glacial system in the U.S., with 35% of the park covered by glaciers. During the cruise into Yakutat Bay, which narrows into Disenchantment Bay, you may see humpback whales, orcas, bald eagles, seals, sea lions and even bears on shore. Most ships have naturalists on board to help with (and announce) wildlife sightings during the ship's visit to the bay. It's part of a national park and preserve covering over 3 million acres and encompassing more than 1,000 glaciers, seven of which are tidewater glaciers you can see from the ship. Cunard, Holland America, Norwegian, Princess, Seabourn, Viking, American Cruise Lines, Lindblad, UnCruise and Alaskan Dream Cruises. The obvious wow is that you can see seven glaciers in one day here. Also cool is that the bay is part of a national park, and rangers will board the ship to answer your questions. They’ll have maps, charts and all the information you could want about the park's glaciers and wildlife. Yes, you can even get your national park passport stamped. The ship will visit the park for nine to 10 hours, traveling more than 120 miles. I found itineraries that started as early as 6 a.m. and one on Holland America that arrived at 8:30 a.m. (It stayed until 6:30 p.m.) Ships stop in front of one of the tidewater glaciers for about an hour, rotating 360 degrees to give everyone on board a view. Only two large cruise ships are allowed per day; luckily, the park classifies smaller lines — including UnCruise, Lindblad and American Cruise Lines — as tour vessels rather than cruise ships, so the big-ship limits don’t apply. Throughout the day of cruising, you can expect to see harbor seals, Steller sea lions, sea otters and bald eagles. You may also see brown bears (coastal grizzlies), black bears, humpback whales, harbor porpoises, mountain goats, orcas and puffins. Which is better: Hubbard Glacier or Glacier Bay? For length of time spent scenic cruising: Glacier Bay wins this one. The limited number of ships allowed each day means it is an all-day event for the lucky few who cruise these waters. Cruises to Hubbard Glacier typically spend a few hours near the glacier. For dramatic presentation: Hubbard Glacier is the drama queen of all Alaskan glaciers. Between its brilliant blue colors, thunderous calving and monumental size, Hubbard puts on quite a show. The glaciers in Glacier Bay are quieter, far less flashy and less likely to exhibit calving of large ice chunks. For wildlife viewing: Both scenic glacier cruises put you in ideal spots to see Alaskan wildlife and sea life throughout the visit; however, Glacier Bay is the winner because ships stay in the bay longer. It's like having an extended wildlife viewing excursion — except you never have to leave the ship. For children or those with short attention spans: Hubbard wins here because it's a shorter visit. A visit to Glacier Bay is a long, slow affair, often beginning early in the morning and requiring warm clothing and lots of patience. The one plus for kids at Glacier Bay is interaction with the park rangers on board the ship. For choice of cruise lines: Hubbard for the win here also. I tracked down 16 different cruise lines offering Hubbard stops in their itineraries. Glacier Bay does earn bonus points, though, for having the greatest number of small-ship options. Imagine the thrill of cruising here on board an UnCruise, Lindblad or American Cruise Lines vessel. For cruise cost: Both glacier stops are likely to require a one-way itinerary, which can add to your airfare costs, but Glacier Bay edges out Hubbard on this one. This is primarily because we did find a handful of seven-night, round-trip itineraries that included stops here. Also, for the best viewing at Hubbard, you may still need a shore excursion on a smaller boat, which will add to your total cost. Most likely to succeed: This one is also a win for Glacier Bay. With seven glaciers, the odds are stacked in your favor. It would take severe weather, dense fog or a ship emergency to keep you from seeing at least one glacier within this park on your itinerary. Other glaciers in Alaska to see by cruise ship While Hubbard and Glacier Bay are the two most famous glacier choices on Alaska cruises, don't forget the smaller options. If your itinerary says you'll be cruising in Tracy Arm Fjord, you are there to see the twin Sawyer glaciers. The narrow fjord is stunning in its beauty. Plus, you'll get closer to land here than in the big open bays, offering a better view of waterfalls and wildlife. Look for bears and mountain goats. MSC’s first season in Alaska includes cruising time in Tracy Arm. Endicott Arm is a fjord that branches off Tracy Arm and might be used as a backup if the weather or ice prevents your ship from reaching the Sawyer glaciers. Because Endicott Arm is a bit straighter than Tracy Arm, larger ships (such as Royal Caribbean's Anthem of the Seas and Ovation of the Seas) will schedule visits here. The glacier you'll see at Endicott Arm is Dawes Glacier, which is the destination listed on Disney Cruise Line's Alaska itineraries. Ships may offer boat excursions to see these glaciers close-up, both on the day of scenic cruising and in Juneau, Alaska. Windstar Cruises’ Star Seeker itineraries use Zodiac excursions for close-up views of these glaciers. College Fjord is a more northerly option near Whittier, Alaska, so you'll typically find it on itineraries that sail to or from Whittier or Seward, Alaska. This is a bonus glacier-viewing spot because most itineraries that include it also include either Hubbard Glacier or Glacier Bay. The real bonus, though, is that the fjord is home to five tidewater glaciers. You can enjoy an Alaska cruise without seeing glaciers. However, if that's an important part of your dream Alaska experience, you should book a cruise with more than one opportunity to see glaciers because things can (and do) go wrong. As for choosing Hubbard Glacier or Glacier Bay, our vote goes to Glacier Bay for ease of viewing, time spent in front of the glaciers and cost to visit — but you won't be disappointed with either option. item.title: Glen and Bessie Hyde Set Out to Break a Grand Canyon Record. They Were Never Heard from Again.
item.description:
Source: Outside Magazine
Glen and Bessie Hyde photographed in their sweep boat on the Colorado River in the Grand Canyon, 1928 (Photo: Northern Arizona University) On October 20, 1928, Glen and Bessie Hyde set off on the Colorado River to break a world record. In a boat Glen built himself, the newlyweds attempted a speed-record paddle from Green River, Utah, down the Colorado River through the Grand Canyon. The record would have made Bessie the first woman to run this stretch of water—except that shortly after they launched, the two mysteriously disappeared. The couple was last seen alive on November 18, 1928. Three weeks later, rescuers found their abandoned, fully loaded boat near river mile 237. Their bodies were never recovered. Peter Runge, a historian at Northern Arizona University, told Outside that the Hyde disappearance remains one of the Grand Canyon’s most perplexing unsolved cases. “Everyone loves a good mystery, and this particular story has been so mysterious because there are no answers,” Runge said. Although nobody knows what happened to the couple, Runge said the archives hold some clues. In 1996, author Brad Dimock published a book about the Hyde mystery titled Sunk Without a Sound. He describes Glen as an experienced outdoorsman who rowed the Salmon and Snake Rivers in Idaho. He met Bessie while traveling on a passenger ship from San Francisco to Los Angeles in 1925, and they married the following April—just six months before setting off on what would become a record-breaking descent. Glen was 29 when they disappeared; Bessie was 22. November can be a volatile time in the Grand Canyon, with chilly nights and mornings, unexpected rain, wind, and sometimes low-elevation snow. Today, a standard river trip through the Grand Canyon runs 277 river miles, lasts 14 to 26 days, and begins at Lee’s Ferry and ends at Diamond Creek or near Pearce Ferry. It has 250 whitewater rapids, each ranked by difficulty. “The Colorado River is a really dangerous place,” Runge said. “A lot of people go down there and make it through just fine, but that’s in part because of the skill and acumen of all the river runners, guides, sampers, and all those folks keeping everybody safe.” At the time of their voyage, however, the Colorado River was undammed. Runge said this pre-dammed environment was extremely hazardous. “It was a really challenging trip,” Runge said. “Looking at the visual evidence, the photographs, in the first few photos of Bessie that we have available online, you can see excitement early on. As the trip continues, there’s less and less in her eyes and facial expressions.” In the last known photo taken of Bessie, she looks tired and worn out, according to Runge. This could have been partly due to their gear. A photograph of Glen and Bessie at the foot of Bright Angel Trail shows them wearing heavy leather, wool, and fur jackets that, if wet, would have made it difficult to move and swim freely. They also weren’t wearing life jackets, and if they had swum, their clothes would have weighed them down even more in the turbulent river. Glen designed and built the 20-foot wooden sweep boat named Rain-in-the-Face. Unlike a rowboat or raft, a sweep boat has oars at the bow and stern. These large blades sweep the water from the bow and stern to counterbalance the boat. Because of this design, the oars don’t propel the boat forward; instead, they change the boat’s angle as it moves downstream. Sweep boats were widely used in the 1880s because they efficiently transport heavy freight on calmer waters, and they’re still used in parts of Idaho today. “The boat that Glen built, the scow, was perfectly designed for other waters, not the Colorado River,” Runge said. “The style of boat that he constructed was common up in the Pacific Northwest, but not common down on the Colorado River. The Colorado River has rapids that were much more robust than those up in the Pacific Northwest.” According to Runge, the cumbersome design could have caused the boat to hit a rapid or an underwater rock formation and, at the moment of impact, bucked the couple from their vessel. “The scow is almost as if it’s a coffin without a lid,” Runge said. “As the boat was going downriver, it’s likely it hit that rock formation just beneath the surface of the water, and Glen and Bessie were thrown from the boat. Everything, all of their belongings, was found on the boat—cameras and diaries—the only things missing were Glen and Bessie.” The river-running community remains fascinated by the Hyde mystery nearly a century later, and conspiratorial theories about what happened have pushed into modern culture According to Dimock’s book, in 1971, a woman named Elizabeth Cutler claimed to be Bessie and alleged that she had stabbed her husband during a fight before abandoning their boat and hiking out of the Grand Canyon. Cutler later recanted, and no evidence supported her story. Another theory centered on Georgie White, a pioneering river runner who became the first woman to own a commercial rafting business in the Grand Canyon. After her death in 1992, investigators reportedly found the Hydes’ wedding license and a birth certificate identifying Clark as Bessie DeRoss among her belongings, according to Northern Arizona University. However, the theory has a major flaw: Clark’s timeline does not align with Bessie Hyde’s disappearance. “It’s very unlikely Georgie was Bessie,” Runge said. White began exploring the Grand Canyon in 1945 after her 15-year-old daughter was struck and killed by a driver. She has her own sad and tragic story, but it’s not this one.” A third theory emerged after investigators discovered a skeleton in the garage of Emery Kolb, a Grand Canyon photographer and early canyon resident, following his death. Kolb captured their final photograph on November 18 and later helped search for the Hydes. The remains, believed to have been found around 1919, were accompanied by clothing fragments and a canvas canoe suspended from the rafters. In 1980, an Arizona Daily Sun article speculated that the bones might belong to one of the Hydes. But a medical examiner identified the skeleton as that of a young man, approximately six feet tall, with a bullet lodged in his skull. An Associated Press report the following year suggested the remains could be Glen. No evidence supported the theory, and the case remained unresolved, according to the National Park Service. What we know is that the lack of answers, the absence of recovered bodies, and river guides’ storytelling keep the legend alive. “The river-running community loves a good mystery, and they love a good story, and they never let the truth get in the way of telling a good story,” said Runge, who’s rowed the Colorado River himself. “When you’re going down the river, part of the experience is the stories that river guides share with their passengers—scientific, geological, environmental, but also cultural and social.” Bessie still holds the record for becoming the first woman to run Cataract Canyon and much of the Grand Canyon.

item.title: REVIEW: Review: Rab Microlite Alpine Down Jacket
item.description:
Source: Sectionhiker.com
The Rab Microlite Alpine Down Jacket is a lightweight, versatile mountain jacket for hiking, climbing, ski touring, camping, and everyday winter use. Its main strengths are its fantastic hiker-centric hood, weather-resistant down, and relatively low weight. - Insulation: 700-fill-power recycled down with Nikwax hydrophobic, fluorocarbon-free treatment - Actual Weight: 442 g / 15.6 oz in men’s size L - Hood: Adjustable, down-filled hood with a stiffened peak, designed to work under a climbing helmet - Pockets: 3 zippered (2 hand, 1 chest) - Fabric: 30-denier Pertex Quantum nylon with DWR water resistance - Packable: Yes, into each of the jacket’s three pockets The hood on the Rab Microlite is one of the jacket’s most useful features for serious outdoor use. It includes a stiffened peak and high neck that help shield the face from wind and precipitation, while interior toggles let the wearer adjust the hood size around the face. There’s a zipper garage at the top and soft microfiber fabric for added face and chin comfort. This level of functionality in a down jacket hood at this price point is unheard of, and you’ll appreciate it if you’re belaying your partner or hiking up an exposed ridge in blowing snow. If you’ve been frustrated by the lack of hood adjustability on similar down jackets or by oversized hoods that assume you’re wearing a climbing or ski helmet, the Rab Microlite hood is the antidote. It is designed to fit under a hood and is optimized for users like hikers who aren’t wearing one. The 30D Pertex Quantum shell is wind-resistant and treated with a durable water repellent finish. It’s not as thin or lightweight as the 7D shell fabrics used on ultralight down jackets on purpose, but it’s designed for increased tear resistance and durability for everyday use as well as outdoor pursuits. It handles light showers, mist, and brief exposure to damp conditions, but it isn’t waterproof. The jacket’s sewn-through baffles keep it slim and flexible, but they don’t provide as much loft or heat retention as the box-wall construction in heavier or more expensive down jackets. The 700-fill power hydrophobic down balances warmth, compressibility, and durability. The jacket is not designed as an expedition-weight parka, but it offers enough insulation for cool-weather camping, hiking, and general mountain use. While you can buy lighter jackets with higher fill-power down, they often sacrifice hood performance. At 422 g (15.6 oz) in men’s size large, the Microlight Alpine is light enough for backpacking and climbing without being among the lightest down jackets available. Its compact baffle design and lightweight outer fabric compress easily into a backpack, making it a dependable emergency layer or camp jacket. The Microlight Alpine uses recycled materials for its main components, including the outer fabric, lining, and down insulation. Rab’s recycled down is recovered from post-consumer duvets and garments that would otherwise be discarded. The down also receives a hydrophobic treatment intended to reduce moisture absorption and help it retain warmth in damp conditions. The Microlight Alpine has a roomy cut, articulated sleeves, and slightly longer arms to support reaching and climbing movements. Its longer hem extends below the belt line, helping prevent the jacket from riding up beneath a climbing harness. The usual size should work well over a base layer or light fleece, while sizing up may be preferable if you plan to wear a thick midlayer underneath. The Rab Microlight Alpine Down Jacket is a well-balanced down jacket for active outdoor use. It combines moderate weight, useful three-season warmth, a functional helmet-compatible hood, and recycled materials in a durable package. It is particularly suitable for hiking, backpacking, climbing, ski touring, travel, and everyday winter layering. For users who want one versatile down jacket for a wide range of mountain and outdoor activities, the Microlight Alpine remains a strong choice. Difference Between This Model and Newest Release Rab just introduced a new version of this jacket (late 2026) that is identical to the old one, except for the materials used. The old jacket used 100% recycled down treated with Nikwax water resistance, while the new version uses a treatment from Granger. Similarly, the old version used a 100% recycled 30D Pertex Quantum shell, while the new version uses a slightly different 100% recycled 30D Pertex Quantum made from recycled fishing nets. Otherwise, the functionality is identical. SectionHiker never accepts payment for gear reviews or editorial coverage. When you buy through affiliate links on our site, we may earn a small commission at no extra cost to you. Help us continue to test and write unsponsored and independent gear reviews, hiking and backpacking FAQs, and free hiking guides.

item.title: IDEA: Finland is giving away 16 free trips to singles, but is the 'happiest country' also the most romantic?
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler UK
The Nordic countries are well known for their rather gimmicky yet innovative travel campaigns luring travellers to the icy north. From doctors prescribing Sweden as a cure to Oslo sharing a mock-documentary narrated by a jaded local called Halfdan, complaining about how easy and available the city is. Preceding these by a decade, Danish tour operator Spies Travels ran a ”Do It for Denmark!” campaign focused on Denmark’s low birth rates, offering ovulation discounts to couples who proved they conceived on their romantic trip. Now, Finland wants you to have some Finnish – literally, figuratively and physically. Finland is wearing its heart on its sleeve and vulnerably putting itself out there to court you. With its new tongue-in-cheek “Love At First Bite” campaign, Finland will fly in sixteen international singles during the throes of winter come February. The country is touting it as the most epic blind dinner date ever, designed to help participants “discover Finnish food, meet new people, and perhaps even find love.” The singles will be divided and hosted in two exclusive group dates in capital city Helsinki and Tampere located in Europe’s largest lake district, Finland’s Lakeland region. They’ll tuck into Finnish gastronomy, drawing heavily on seasonal ingredients. Joining the singles over candlelit tasting menus crafted by local celebrity chefs will be everyday Finns. Get ready for lots of prolonged eye contact – the Nordic way of flirting – under low light as you bond over the likes of wild trout, reindeer, chanterelle mushrooms and sea buckthorn. For those heading to Tampere, it is monikered the ‘world’s sauna capital,’ so chances of after-dinner relaxation in the most intimate way with a stranger are very high and probably on the menu too. I’ll admit, when the campaign was launched worldwide, my Finnish friends and I wrinkled our noses in confusion. ‘Romantic’ and ‘sexy’ aren’t the first words that come to mind when you think of Finland. And it's not the Nordic country you'd first go to for love if we're talking stereotypes. The Danes have their extroverted charm, the Swedes their chic worldliness, and the Norwegians typically have more money to spend on you. Popular Nordic comedians Helgi and Erlend riff on these regional stereotypes, depicting their Finnish character as stoic, quiet and mentally tough. The very Finnish ethos of sisu means grit and the tenacity to push through tough times. Maybe those are qualities you'd want in a lifelong partner as you navigate challenges together. So the campaign got me thinking a little deeper. Named the happiest country in the world for the ninth consecutive year in a row, Finns are satisfied with their lifestyles firmly rooted in the outdoors, nature and a slower pace of life. In this contentment is where you’ll find Finland’s hidden sexier side. In a country of roughly five million, there are two million saunas. And a few places are more intimate than sweating together naked in a sauna, dipping in chilly lakes during winter, then warming back up indoors in many more ways. There’s also something rather romantic about grilling wild-caught salmon for two over an open flame in the backcountry. This isn’t the first time the country has dabbled in an unconventional approach to dating. Its viral Sinkkukori phenomenon introduced pink shopping baskets as a way for singles to covertly signal their availability. Now Finland is taking a more overt approach to romance. As the well-known nineteenth-century English idiom reminds us, the quickest way to the heart is through the stomach, and Finland certainly wants to put this to the test. Want to apply for your shot at Finnish love? All you have to do is make a video answering the question: what would you serve on a dinner date, and why? Just like a proper prospect, Finland would like to know your preferences in advance so it can woo you in the most epic and intentional way. If that isn’t romantic, I don’t know what is.

item.title: REVIEW: Of All the Cookware, BA Editors Keep Coming Back to These Made In Products
item.description:
Source: Bon Appétit
We've all heard the old adage “If it ain't broke, don''t fix it" and that rings particularly true in the kitchen. Because when you're scrambling on a Tuesday night to get dinner on the stove, or ambitiously experimenting with a dessert recipe to show off at your annual Friendsgiving, you need your favorite cookware to show up. These are not the moments to be re-inventing the cookware-wheel. Perhaps this is why BA staffers keep coming back these Made In pieces. They just work. When so much else can go sideways mid food-project (was that cup of sugar a few grams off? Did that bread dough proof all the way??), having tools that do what they're supposed to do gives us one less thing to worry about. As much as we love testing new gear (it’s literally our job), Made In has earned a permanent spot in our the rotation of our writers and editors. What our writers and editors say: “It’s the only pan I reach for when I want to make eggs and quesadillas." - Emily Farris, contributing writer The CeramiClad Non-stick frying pan was my first “grown-up” piece of cookware I ever invested in, and years later, it's still one of my most reached for pans in my cabinet. Other editors love it too; in her review, contributor Emily Farris claims it got her to break up with Teflon for good. She said the slick, ceramic coating made quick work of eggs and quesadillas, while the five-ply base gives it a sturdier feel and even heat distribution. It’s also impressively easy to clean with nothing more than a soft sponge and soapy water. Just stick to low or medium heat, skip the metal utensils, and wash it by hand to help preserve that nonstick surface. What our writers and editors say: "Made In’s baking slab has brought some much needed crunch in my life." - Noah Kaufman, senior reviews editor Why we love it: If you’re someone who fights for as much of the crispy top of a baked pasta as you can get, then you will love this baking slab. In his review, Noah Kaufman found that Made In’s shallow, 9-by-13-inch porcelain slab delivers more of the hard, crispy edges that make baked dishes so satisfying. Its low sides also make it much easier to slide a spatula underneath desserts like blondies and bars without mangling the whole thing. Kaufman put it to work on everything from fudgy brownies to baked mac n' cheese with excellent results. It won’t replace a deep casserole dish for every recipe, but for the shallower bakes where you want a satisfying crunch on top, this slab slays. What our writers and editors say: “I’m officially retiring my traditional saucepan in favor of this saucier.” - Olivia Tarantino, senior reviews editor A saucier might just look like an uppity saucepan, but its rounded bottom really does make it especially useful for whisking, stirring, and tossing. Last November, our senior commerce editor Olivia Tarantino got her hands on this 5-quart version and fell in love. The five-ply stainless steel has excellent heat transfer and retention, which helped delicate scrambled eggs cook without sticking. She also loved it for pasta, where its curved sides made it easy to toss noodles with sauce until every strand is coated in a silky finish. It was so impressive that she ditched her old saucepan in favor of it—which is about as strong an endorsement as a piece can get. What our writers and editors say: “I wasn’t shocked at how much I enjoyed using the Made In Dutch oven—I just didn’t expect to reach for it as often as I do.” - EF Le Creuset and Staub have long dominated the Dutch oven game, but Made In makes a compelling case for spending less on an heirloom piece without sacrificing quality. In her side-by-side review, Farris found that the brand’s enameled cast-iron pot held its own against both legacy favorites, with a similarly sturdy build and smooth interior. Its wide, flat side handles are a particular standout, offering plenty of surface area for lifting the heavy pot off the stove or out of the oven. Available in a 5.5-quart size, you can use it for braises, soups, and even sourdough—and it won't completely drain your wallet like the other brands might. What our writers and editors say: “I can't get over how well this thing sears food from edge to edge. And the fact that you can transform just about any cooking surface into a griddle makes it even better.” - Francesca Krempa, contributor I yearn for a giant Blackstone but don't have the space, which is why I love Made In's carbon steel griddle set. It delivers that flat-top experience on a much smaller footprint, with even heating and a seasoned cooking surface that’s prime for searing smash burgers, fried rice, and more. It’s also lighter than cast iron, so it’s easier to lift and shift around, and comes pre-seasoned (hallelujah). Best of all, you can turn a compatible stovetop or cooking surface into a griddle without dedicating precious patio real estate to a massive piece of equipment. Just measure your stovetop before buying, since the integrated handles may not fit every range. Tom Colicchio x Made In Carbon Steel Frying Pan What our writers and editors say: "I love the way the handle feels: It gives good leverage for tossing and keeps your hands far from any splattering oil if you’re moving it into the oven." - NK Limited-edition cookware can sometimes feel more like a collector’s item than something you’d actually want to cook with, but this collab has the performance to back up its celebrity partnership. In BA’s October editor-favorites roundup, Kaufman praised this pre-seasoned black steel pan for its striking brass handle and thicker construction that makes it easier to get a deep, even sear. What our writers and editors say: “They're a splurge but if you love to grill, they're worth it." - FK I’m a sucker for kitchen tools that balance function with good design, and Made In’s stainless steel grill tools hit that sweet spot. The sturdy stainless steel heads can handle the usual cookout lineup, from flipping burgers to turning vegetables, while the composite handles add a warm, classic touch that looks right at home next to the grill. The handles, which are made from a material called Micarta, a composite that looks like wood but is as maintenance-heavy. Plus they're more comfortable in-hand than all-metal tools. They're a splurge, but if you love to grill, they're worth it. What our writers and editors say: “More than two years in, my Made In flatware has taken hundreds of trips through the dishwasher and my kids have slammed it onto our granite countertop more times than I’d like to admit—and it still looks great.” - EF Farris dubbed this her “forever flatware” and it's easy to see why. Made In’s 18/10 stainless steel (read: very durable) set struck the right balance between substantial weight and comfy handling. The mirror-polished finish and understated curves look polished enough for a dinner party without feeling too precious for everyday meals. It's not cheap, but its timeless design and impressive durability make it a smart long-term investment for anyone ready to retire their mismatched drawer of utensils.

item.title: IDEA: I Hiked the B Side of Italy’s Famous Pilgrim Trail
item.description:
Source: Outside Magazine
To my right were the Apuan Alps, scarred white from two thousand years of marble mining. To my left, a few miles off, the sea. And directly beneath me: asphalt, a narrow shoulder, and the persistent attentiveness of not getting clipped by Fiat Pandas and silent electric Citroëns. I was walking a stretch of the Via Francigena, the medieval pilgrim route that runs from Canterbury to Rome, from Camaiore to Sarzana. It’s, how do you say, gritty Tuscany. This is not the Tuscany of postcards. In Carrara I got the industry of marble instead: giant cubes of it hoisted by cranes, sitting in open lots like unclaimed luggage, waiting to become countertops in bougie kitchen remodels. Less likely to become the next David. I’d come to meet a friend at the 100-mile mark of her Via Francigena walk, a centerpiece of her sabbatical; I’d do the next 50 or so miles with her. Which is to say I didn’t really look into what I was getting myself into. I was along for the ride no matter what. If I’d pictured anything, it was the Tuscany she’d been describing from the trail for weeks. South of Siena, the route rolls through the Val d’Orcia and the Crete Senesi with its white gravel roads, cypress-lined ridgelines, as well as San Quirico, Radicofani perched on its volcanic cone. North of Siena you get the stunning San Gimignano and Monteriggioni. The stuff that launched a thousand Under-the-Tuscan-Sun fantasies. The Via Francigena is roughly 1,250 miles and, at a pace of 12 to 15 miles per hour, per day, takes about 90 days. Few attempt that. Most walk a section that for one- or two-weeks, usually in Tuscany, and revisit it over a lifetime. Many just do the final 60 or so miles into Rome, the minimum on foot to earn the Testimonium, the official completion certificate, which is why the last stages are the most crowded. If my friend’s stretch was the greatest hits of the Via, this would be the B side. I had gotten a taste of the more genteel school of pilgrimage walking on the Camino de Santiago a stretch of hiking routes that are primarily in Spain, with chef and humanitarian José Andrés. A slow pace during the day, long lunches, even longer dinners. And I’ve made peace with my position on this spectrum: I like the idea of roughing it in a hut. I also like putting on clean clothes at night and being a tourist. There is a slang term for this kind of Camino walking that applies to the Via Francigena as well: turigrino, a Spanish mashup of turista (tourist) and peregrino (which roughly translates to pilgrim or someone who wanders to distant lands). It’s sort of a pejorative, at least if you ask the more Type 2 end of the spectrum. But I like clean clothes and a nice cold glass of bubbly Franciacorta at the end of the day. I would not, it turned out, be getting the full turigrino treatment. The morning before my flight, my friend called. She’d been slackpacking most of her trip. That’s where you walk with a daypack while a service ferries your real luggage ahead to the next hotel. But she’d searched hard, asked around, and on our stretch, no such service existed. Mentally, I pivoted from a Type 2 Light vacation–walking with some water and some gummy bears to Type 2 Heavy: walking with everything. Fine, except I was leaving in 12 hours and my actual backpacks were all in storage. There would be no run to REI. I went with what I had: a running hydration pack/vest with slightly ambitious storage, never once worn, missing one of its two chest straps. I hated that pack. Then I hated it some more. Then I accepted it the way you accept a blister. Starting out, it felt terrible; eventually you resign yourself to the terribleness, and somewhere past that resignation. Around day three I arrived at something like affection, the Stockholm-syndrome phase of gear ownership. I will still probably give it away. Nobody tells you about the unfashionable stretch of a famous walk: nobody is on it. Over the entire leg we encountered perhaps six other hikers. Everyone else we passed was simply living their life because, well, they lived there. For days, we seemed to be the only tourists in Italy, a feeling that, if you’ve ever bottlenecked your way through the ancient streets of Florence or Rome in summer, you know is supposed to be impossible. The numbers back the feeling up. Even in 2025, which was a Jubilee year in Rome and the best year in the Via’s modern history, only about 12,000 people collected a Testimonium, and the route’s governing association estimated that roughly 100,000 set foot on some piece of its 2,000 kilometers all year. The Camino de Santiago issued 530,919 Compostelas in the same twelve months. The Via is growing fast, with completions roughly doubling in each of the past two years. But it’s growing from almost nothing, which makes it, for now, a rare thing for Italy: a famous place that’s not overrun with tourists. In Carrara, your mind wanders in two directions at once. What would these mountains look like if they’d never been mined? The scars are obvious, bright white, visible from the sea. But then: What would the world look like without the David, the Pietà, London’s Marble Arch? Beauty still presents itself, even if it’s not as obvious as a postcard. My notes and photos from this trip conjure more poetic memories. Bay laurel crushed between my fingers, smelling like adobo about to happen. Fresh-foraged mint chewed on the trail. Queen Anne’s lace, which I can now report does in fact sort of taste like carrots. Blackberries that seemed to materialize precisely when you needed a little sweetness. My first pomegranate on the tree. Chestnuts in their spiny husks, which make them look like terrestrial sea urchins, which I’d first met on the Camino with José. An olive grove leaning over the trail, depositing pits from last year’s harvest, or the year before that, or before that. Redwoods are awesome, but there’s something magical about the longevity of an olive tree. And always, up ahead, another hilltop town with its own strange story of how it came to be. And then there was the dining, which on this stretch requires zero effort, zero reservations, and zero contending with other tourists. Baccalà and a primo of cacciagione in Camaiore. In Seravezza, a rustic seafood risotto, salted like the sea a few miles off, and better for it. In Massa, maltagliati cut from corn flour, known locally as curchua, and at a restaurant called Origine, calamarata, fat rings of pasta doing an impression of the calamari they’re named for, tangled with prawns, followed by polpo over a cassava mousseline with gremolata: a plate more Milan than marble town. This is the journey I will remember as getting hooked on Franciacorta—Italy’s answer to Champagne. So much better than Prosecco, so rarely seen in the States. I made a nightly ritual of it. Every table around us was locals, eating where they always eat. The crescendo came at Locanda de’ Banchieri, a one-time Malaspina residence that spent centuries as a post station taxing the marble trade out of Luni’s ancient port, now a Michelin-starred inn run by Giacomo Devoto, a chef from Sarzana. This is where our walk would end. With wood-fired bread under a ragout and butter of Tuscan black kale. Croxetti, coin-like Ligurian pasta, in a white pesto of San Rossore pine nuts and marjoram. A kitchen doing what we’d been doing by accident for days: taking in the landscape. Even the cars, in the end, weren’t so bad. My most memorable encounter of the whole walk was a shirtless old-timer easing past me in an ancient Fiat pickup who smiled, raised a hand, and offered a single word: “Calma.” The walking is still walking, even when you’re not putting in the full miles, and that’s okay. Few people talk about the low-grade boredom of these paths—the long connective tissue of road shoulder you endure to get to the things that are photo-worthy. But maybe that’s the ratio of any trip worth taking. It can’t be a screensaver all the time. And would you even want that, in Italy, where the too-perfect is always too crowded? The crowds sort themselves to the pretty parts. The rest they leave to you. Calma.
